Treasury Yields Resume Their Rise
 
Plus, oil’s streak ends and McDonald’s outlines a spending plan
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
MIKE SEGAR/REUTERS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Stock indexes dropped sharply as yields surged. The S&P 500 fell 0.8%, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 352 points, or 0.7%. Higher Treasury yields raise the bar for equity returns with investors, particularly with growth stocks.

 

Crude oil broke its losing streak. Brent crude futures moved back above $100, ending a five-session decline. Brent prices rose almost 4%, to $103.08 a barrel. This came despite talks between U.S. and Iranian representatives on the sidelines of a U.N. meeting. A potential U.S. diesel export ban is exacerbating supply crunch worries in Europe.

 

Ten-year Treasury yields hit 5.1%. The 10-year yield rose almost 0.15 percentage point, to 5.113%. Oil’s price rise accompanied firming conviction that the Fed will be hiking again. A pickup in S&P Global’s U.S. purchasing-managers’ index also helped fueled rate-hike expectations. CME Group’s FedWatch tracking on Wednesday showed the likelihood of an October hike going from 55% yesterday to closer to 70%. Fed governor Michael Barr said he expects further rate increases, and a five-year Treasury auction was met with weak demand.

 

McDonald’s shares dropped on franchisee plan. The company said it will spend $8.5 billion to help its store owners invest in equipment and operations so they can keep up with fast-food rivals. McDonald’s shares fell nearly 5%.

One Big Story

 
 
DAVID PAUL MORRIS/BLOOMBERG
 

The number of smartphones and personal computers sold this year is on track for a major decline. But for the manufacturers of those devices, that may not matter.

 

Even as unit shipments fall, analysts expect device revenue to climb this year for smartphone players Samsung Electronics and Apple as well as PC makers Lenovo, Dell Technologies and HP.

 

The main reason for the disconnect between sales and revenue are memory chip prices, which are being driven higher by the AI race. Faced with higher input costs, manufacturers are raising device prices and keeping revenue elevated.

• Darden Restaurants and Costco Wholesale are reporting quarterly earnings.

 

• Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, who is a Federal Open Market Committee voter this year, is speaking.

 

• There be economic data from the Kansas City Fed’s September survey and a release of new-home sales for August.
